look_here_first: TEXAS BLUEGRASS — native cool-season RHIZOMATOUS perennial and DIOECIOUS (female and male flowering plants separate). First see the source-photographed FEMALE spikelet basal cobwebs (Harms POAR-F2/FS), then the real MEMBRANOUS collar ligule (Harms POAR-L). Don't call a grass Texas bluegrass from a boat-shaped leaf tip or hairy-looking flowering head alone. The exact missing crew-confirmation photographs remain the MALE staminate floret and an intact underground RHIZOME linking rooted shoots; the iNaturalist flowering-stand image does not expose roots.

learner_visual_status.note: 2026-10-26: 7 physically installed source-identified species JPEGs (six Bob Harms pistillate reproductive/ligule images; one original iNaturalist field-flowering stand), plus one copyright-retained Bob Harms F4 external-only image. Ten gallery panels total (seven exact species incl. one external; three explicitly other-species P. annua). Six accurate core crew teaching tiles now map to existing panel indices. True male flowers and connected rhizome/roots remain missing. Original NC and Bob Harms legal attribution/publishing scopes unchanged, final Pages not verified.

best_field_traits: Perennial spreading on underground rhizomes forming prairie grass sod, often 20–70 cm high.
Dioecious: male and female florets on separate individuals.
Bright to pale silver flowering heads in spring and smooth sheaths.
Boat-shaped blade tips and a membranous true ligule are genus-level characteristics.

Actual Texas-source photographer Bob Harms macro of female spikelets (POAR-FS) clearly shows long cobwebby basal/floral hairs on photographic mm scale. Avoid unverified arrow to individual attachment/callus.
Actual same-species Bob Harms L photo shows true pale membranous leaf-collar ligule; shared within Poa. Male/mature same-rooted flowering and rhizome evidence still missing.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Connected TEXAS BLUEGRASS rhizome between two living legal specimen ramets, with centimeter ruler; local source/location proven independently.
True sexually separated (male and female) flowering individuals, each observed anthesis and independently keyed; photograph functional anthers or carpels on SAME documented flowering shoots.
Male one-floret and female one-floret dissected with a 1-mm ruler and explicit 4–10 mm female spiderweb threads at lemma callus; new Harms FS serves female reference only, does NOT resolve male.

An independently verified live same-plant Hays blade-sheath junction, 1 mm metric membrane with exact membrane-edge arrows. Harms L is excellent REAL reference but individual actual county / mm tip uncertain.
One truly ripe complete female spikelet in side/face with isolated real glumes, lemma, and rachilla bract labels, photo-verified arrow targets.
crew_field_check: 1 · Look at a source-vouchered adult flowering stand, then a REAL POAR-F PISTILLATE panicle; these original Harms photos are true Poa arachnifera female-source labels, not mere green head guesses.
2 · See PISTILLATE F2 flowering unit close-up; find long airy cobweb-like pale threads around actual pointed green spikelets. These are basal flower/lemma hairs, not stigmas or leaf pubescence.
3 · Inspect PISTILLATE F3 larger cluster showing bract overlap and webbing against a real segmented scale. Never point to a specific glume or the exact tiny callus base without organ isolation.

4 · Identify disassembled FS ACTUAL female spikelets and pale 4–10 mm cobweb threads; source photo includes true scale. Do not present every pointed glume as a seed. This is the KEY diagnostic close-up.
5 · Compare mature F4/F5 dry female flowerheads: cobwebby hairs can shed or become obscure. Brown color alone cannot distinguish male vs female.
6 · Examine species-matched L PHOTO: actual translucent MEMBRANOUS ligule between blade and sheath; Poa annua has a similar membrane and folded boat blade, so this is genus not species proof.

7 · Find actual male plants separately: staminate anthers versus pistillate carpels, flower stage and compatible morphology on separately photographed site-vouchered specimens. Male Poa arachnifera can ALSO have sparse basal webbing; do not say 'male = never webby'.

8 · Confirm truly connected slender underground rhizomes between living rooted ramets on a legally collected specimen. Do not use one basal dense tuft as proof. Compare bisexual annual P. annua and perennial bisexual P. pratensis.

9 · Crew teach-back: identify at least a true PISTILLATE spikelet and its threadlike basal web, actual LIGULE tissue, reproductive SEX (independently verified), connected RHIZOME where legally accessible. If unknown, ID as Poa sp. and document source/state range separately.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Both P. annua and Texas bluegrass have a membranous ligule and boat-shaped blade tips, so neither clue identifies the native species. Compare reproductive SEX on individually collected florets and actual connected underground rhizomes on same-plant clumps. Kentucky bluegrass (P. pratensis) can also be rhizomatous and may have some basal lemma hairs; its flowers are bisexual, so woolliness alone does not prove P. arachnifera.
not_reliable_alone: Boat-shaped grass leaf tip is a genus trait common to both Poa species
One very green or woolly head photographed at a distance, without sex/lemma macro
Ligule without the complete rooted specimen
Treating state native range as a Hays county voucher

visual_comparison.memory_rule: TEXAS BLUEGRASS: a creeping RHIZOMATOUS perennial with separate FEMALE and MALE plants. Female florets have actual long COBWEBBY BASAL HAIRS around the lemmas: see isolated true female spikelets in POAR-FS. White true MEMBRANE ligule in POAR-L is Poa GENUS support, not itself a species split.

items.label: NEW · TRUE TEXAS BLUEGRASS LIGULE — opened leaf/sheath and ruler · PROVISIONAL USER PHOTO REVIEW
items.image_role: True original Texas Poa arachnifera anatomy triptych of attached leaf blade and sheath, with pale membranous ligule at blade/sheath junction and black/white real scale; no auricles. Left view unopened/side, center and right opened sheath with white upright membrane parts.
items.caption: THIS PHOTO IS TEXAS BLUEGRASS, NOT ANNUAL BLUEGRASS. Bob Harms shows three close views of the actual blade/sheath junction. The thin translucent pale membrane protrudes upward from the top of the green sheath, and the original black-white scale is visible along the side. The central white spike is ligule tissue, NOT a grass awn. Length needs independent pixel-calibrated verification.

items.label: Annual bluegrass — original source photo
items.image_role: Actually visually inspected local JPEG; taxon determination from original source
items.caption: Whole plant photo shows low flowering grass, green leaves, and flowering branches. Neither microscopic lemma characters nor ligule is resolvable.
items.why_it_matters: INTRODUCED annual bluegrass: soft low light-green grass in lawns and paths with small open pale green panicles; folded emerging blades with boat-prow tips and a translucent short membranous ligule. Usually annual, though persistent biotypes occur. True flowers are generally bisexual, unlike dioecious Texas bluegrass.
items.creator: Harry Rose (Macleay Grass Man)

items.label: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — boat-prow shaped leaf tip
items.image_role: Flickr/Commons macro photographed in Pasadena at 30×, identified by original photographer as annual bluegrass; illustrates the boat-shaped folded grass leaf TIP, shared by other Poa, not a species diagnostic.
items.caption: The green blade narrows to a blunt folded, keel-like 'prow' tip. The lightened very tip is visible; it may be a worn or dry margin, not a separate auricle. The photographer reported magnification 30×, but supplied no calibrated ruler. This proves the shared Poa leaf tip shape, not annual versus Texas bluegrass.
items.why_it_matters: This is an actual photograph of the genus recognition clue that the former whole-plant picture could not resolve. The tip belongs to Poa annua per source label, but its shape alone never distinguishes P. annua from Texas bluegrass.

items.label: ANNUAL BLUEGRASS — actual membranous ligule and blade/sheath collar
items.image_role: Four-view composite macro of one Austrian source-identified annual-bluegrass blade/sheath junction, with original photographer's genuine 10 mm scale, NOT four individuals.
items.caption: Four source-photo views show the same kind of grass blade/sheath collar. The bottom view exposes the whitish membranous flap (ligule) exactly where green blade separates from the upper sheath. The genuine 10-mm photo scale sits at bottom; do not confuse the entire pale sheath with the ligule or infer its precise size without local measurement.
items.why_it_matters: Teaches the actual part crews must photograph: a thin membranous ligule at the junction, not a tuft of hairs or a leaf tip. Texas bluegrass also has a membranous ligule; the difference lies primarily in reproductive sex and perennial rhizomes.

field_id_finish_pass.stage: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — major pistillate diagnostic photo roles now REAL and scale-backed; source-vouchered male flower and linked rhizome, precise mobile arrows remain unavailable
field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: Native Texas bluegrass, rhizomatous and DIOECIOUS. These seven new Bob Harms source photographs establish an excellent true FEMALE photo lesson: actual dense female flowering panicles, individual cobwebby flower clusters in closeup and genuine separated female spikelets with silky basal threads, plus actual Texas bluegrass ligule/sheath on source ruler. Distinguish from introduced annual P. annua by life history/rootstock and actual flower sex, NOT Poa boat-tip or membrane alone.
field_id_finish_pass.lookalike_comparison: Both P. annua and Texas bluegrass have a membranous ligule and boat-shaped blade tips, so neither clue identifies the native species. Compare reproductive SEX on individually collected florets and actual connected underground rhizomes on same-plant clumps. Kentucky bluegrass (P. pratensis) can also be rhizomatous and may have some basal lemma hairs; its flowers are bisexual, so woolliness alone does not prove P. arachnifera.
photo_targets: Connected TEXAS BLUEGRASS rhizome between two living legal specimen ramets, with centimeter ruler; local source/location proven independently.
True sexually separated (male and female) flowering individuals, each observed anthesis and independently keyed; photograph functional anthers or carpels on SAME documented flowering shoots.
Male one-floret and female one-floret dissected with a 1-mm ruler and explicit 4–10 mm female spiderweb threads at lemma callus; new Harms FS serves female reference only, does NOT resolve male.

An independently verified live same-plant Hays blade-sheath junction, 1 mm metric membrane with exact membrane-edge arrows. Harms L is excellent REAL reference but individual actual county / mm tip uncertain.
One truly ripe complete female spikelet in side/face with isolated real glumes, lemma, and rachilla bract labels, photo-verified arrow targets.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Texas bluegrass: actual photographed female webs and ligule; find male flowers + connected rhizomes
steps: 1 · Look at a source-vouchered adult flowering stand, then a REAL POAR-F PISTILLATE panicle; these original Harms photos are true Poa arachnifera female-source labels, not mere green head guesses.
2 · See PISTILLATE F2 flowering unit close-up; find long airy cobweb-like pale threads around actual pointed green spikelets. These are basal flower/lemma hairs, not stigmas or leaf pubescence.
3 · Inspect PISTILLATE F3 larger cluster showing bract overlap and webbing against a real segmented scale. Never point to a specific glume or the exact tiny callus base without organ isolation.

4 · Identify disassembled FS ACTUAL female spikelets and pale 4–10 mm cobweb threads; source photo includes true scale. Do not present every pointed glume as a seed. This is the KEY diagnostic close-up.
5 · Compare mature F4/F5 dry female flowerheads: cobwebby hairs can shed or become obscure. Brown color alone cannot distinguish male vs female.
6 · Examine species-matched L PHOTO: actual translucent MEMBRANOUS ligule between blade and sheath; Poa annua has a similar membrane and folded boat blade, so this is genus not species proof.

7 · Find actual male plants separately: staminate anthers versus pistillate carpels, flower stage and compatible morphology on separately photographed site-vouchered specimens. Male Poa arachnifera can ALSO have sparse basal webbing; do not say 'male = never webby'.

8 · Confirm truly connected slender underground rhizomes between living rooted ramets on a legally collected specimen. Do not use one basal dense tuft as proof. Compare bisexual annual P. annua and perennial bisexual P. pratensis.

9 · Crew teach-back: identify at least a true PISTILLATE spikelet and its threadlike basal web, actual LIGULE tissue, reproductive SEX (independently verified), connected RHIZOME where legally accessible. If unknown, ID as Poa sp. and document source/state range separately.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Real PISTILLATE POAR-FS / F2 webbing is a useful evidence-backed target species photo; true Poa L membrane is genus-wide. Final species call needs attached/reviewed female floret with sexual morphology and independently documented connected rhizome and male reference.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: 2026-10-26 repository reconciliation: 8 existing media records include SIX physically archived Bob Harms female/collar JPEGs, ONE physically archived original iNaturalist flowering stand (CC BY-NC conditional), and ONE Bob Harms F4 external-only photo. Ten current teaching panels are SEVEN exact-species (six local + one external F4) and THREE different-species Poa annua comparisons. Bob Harms photographs are copyrighted; site science/education use with credit is noted, but prior collection-specific permission memo reviewed external-display-only uses for four DIFFERENT images, not local copying/adaptation here. Preserve archive and clear exact scope before public certification. No male, connected rhizome or local same-voucher lineage photographed. No new JPEG/arrows/site deployment claimed.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · SEE THE FEMALE WEB
field_id_short_tiles.short: Silky cobwebs surround the female spikelets
field_id_short_tiles.details: Start with true Bob Harms, source-labelled Texas bluegrass PISTILLATE heads: panel 0 is the full female panicle; panel 1 shows the web-like pale hairs on green attached spikelets; panel 3 contains separately displayed female reproductive units with a real source scale. The web comes from hairs around the lemma callus, NOT from stigmas or the leaves. Many spiderweb-like strands are visible in the photos, but their exact individual insertion points and measured lengths are not independently arrow-confirmed. This is useful photo evidence, NOT by itself evidence of a Hays-collected voucher.
field_id_short_tiles.status: ACTUAL FEMALE HEAD/WEB PHOTOGRAPHED — fine insertion still unresolved

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · FIND THE TRUE LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Milky membrane between blade and sheath, not an awn
field_id_short_tiles.details: The true P. arachnifera source-photo triptych (panel 6) shows green sheath, the attached blade and pointed upright PALE LIGULE membrane near their inner junction; its one existing arrow is on visible membrane tissue. A Williamson County specimen treatment reports a smooth, milky-translucent 0.5–2 mm membranous ligule; the broader FNA treatment uses about 1–4 mm. Those are PUBLISHED values, not measurements made from this archived image. The pale membrane is NOT an awn, and both annual bluegrass and Kentucky bluegrass may also have membranous ligules. The P. annua collar shown in panel 9 is a different species.
field_id_short_tiles.status: TRUE SPECIES-MATCHED LIGULE PHOTO VISIBLE; physical 1-mm membrane calibration pending

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · CHECK THE SEEDHEAD AND SEX
field_id_short_tiles.short: Female panicles can be webby; male panicles not yet documented
field_id_short_tiles.details: The adult P. arachnifera female head in panel 0 has ascending branches; younger female units in panel 1 are densely webbed. Dry, later-stage female panicle panel 5 may show less conspicuous webbing. Texas bluegrass is dioecious, so separate individual plants bear staminate (male) or pistillate (female) flowers. A genuine male image must show a source-verified plant with functional anthers and a dissected male floret; smoothness alone is insufficient, because male florets can have sparse basal hairs, and old female webs can be worn away. Panel 4 is a source-linked FEMALE dried head, NOT a male.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FEMALE PHOTOS VERIFIED; ACTUAL MALE FLOWER/ANTHER PHOTOS MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · LIFT AND TRACE RHIZOMES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Perennial slender underground connections, not simply dense tillers
field_id_short_tiles.details: Texas bluegrass spreads through slender BELOW-GROUND rhizomes and produces fibrous adventitious roots; this cannot be diagnosed from the flower pictures. The local Williamson County treatment describes horizontal rhizomes commonly about 2 cm beneath the soil, to about 8 cm long and 0.7–1 mm wide. These values are from literature, NOT photographed measurements. On a legitimately sampled plant, lift soil to trace an INTACT horizontal rhizome from one rooted leafy ramet to another; photograph its nodes, bud/sheath, attached roots and a centimeter ruler without severing the connection. A dense rootless aboveground clump proves nothing about a rhizome.
field_id_short_tiles.status: CRITICAL PHOTO GAP — connected rhizome with two living rooted shoots not photographed

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · DISSECT A FEMALE AND A MALE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Female three-web callus versus male sparse-web callus
field_id_short_tiles.details: The separated, author-identified female reproductive units in panel 3 show real long silky strands beside individual bracts, but the photograph does not trace three independent callus webs or distinguish every lemma/glume boundary. Flora of North America describes female calluses as commonly 3-webbed with long (4–10 mm) plicate hairs; male calluses usually glabrous or sparsely webbed, though some can still have hairs. The needed matched set: source-verified female spikelet and male staminate spikelet, separately opened glumes/lemmas and sexual organs, each beside a physical 1-mm scale. Never infer functional sex from hair density alone.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PISTILLATE MICRO PHOTOS AVAILABLE; PAIRED STAMINATE DISSECTION MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · RULE OUT OTHER POA
field_id_short_tiles.short: Boat-shaped leaf tip and ligule only prove you should check Poa
field_id_short_tiles.details: The annual-bluegrass P. annua comparisons in panels 7–9 show a real small whole flowering plant, boat-prow leaf tip and membranous ligule. These photos are explicitly NOT Texas bluegrass. P. annua is commonly annual, lacks connected perennial rhizomes and generally has bisexual flowers. Introduced Kentucky bluegrass (P. pratensis) may be perennial AND rhizomatous, so only the rhizome/boat-tip combination is not enough; compare genuinely dioecious floral anatomy and marked female basal callus webbing. If male flower sex and underground connections cannot be independently established, teach the record as Poa sp. until resolved.
field_id_short_tiles.status: OTHER-SPECIES PHOTO COMPARISON PRESENT; RHIZOME AND MALE-FLORET CONFIRMATION PENDING
